\paragraph{Limitations.}
Repo-level cross-model \cwm{} results are preliminary (DeepSeek-Coder \cwm{} training in progress); \cls{} results are final. The repo-level same-size comparisons each use a single seed (4B-4B and 8B-8B); multi-seed DeepSeek-Coder \cls{} evaluation is in progress. For \cwm{}, validation loss diverges to NaN (DeepSeek-Coder), preventing standard early stopping and requiring checkpoint selection by validation accuracy. No downstream re-repair experiment validates whether per-test diagnostic signals translate to actual fix improvements. Pass-to-pass regression rates are negligible (1.04\% mean, 0\% median), meaning the per-test advantage currently concentrates in fail-to-pass discrimination; regression detection remains untested in practice. Training data comprises synthetic mutations generated by operator-level transformations (operator swap, off-by-one, return value, boundary removal). While prior work has established that synthetic mutants correlate with real fault detection~\cite{andrews2005mutation,just2014mutants}, the coupling is imperfect: real bugs often involve multi-statement changes, semantic misunderstandings, or integration errors that no single mutation operator captures. Our repo-level evaluation partially mitigates this concern by using SWE-bench Verified test cases derived from real pull requests, but the underlying code changes remain synthetic. Transfer to naturally occurring developer bugs is untested. The oracle analysis assumes ground-truth test labels; real-world per-test advantage is upper-bounded by classifier accuracy. Our \cwm{} comparison uses 4--8B LoRA-adapted models; the original Code World Model~\cite{meta2025cwm} uses 32B parameters with mid-training on execution traces, a fundamentally different capacity regime. \cwm{} format collapse at repo-level complexity may not generalize to larger-scale models or full fine-tuning setups. Our rank ablation (Appendix~\ref{app:ablations}) shows that doubling adapter capacity does not resolve the generation bottleneck within our setup, but the gap between rank-32 LoRA and full 32B mid-training is substantial; we do not claim that generation \emph{cannot} succeed at scale, only that it does not under our experimental configuration.

11	\paragraph{\cls{} (per-test classification).} $f(c_p, t_i) \rightarrow \hat{y}_i \in \{\text{\textsc{Pass}}, \text{\textsc{Fail}}\}$ predicts a single binary token per test (cross-entropy loss). Patch verdict: $\hat{y}_p = \bigwedge_{i} [\hat{y}_i = \text{\textsc{Pass}}]$. Output cost: one token per test.

2	Execution-free verification for LLM-based code repair can be formulated in multiple ways, yet no controlled comparison exists across formulations at matched model capacity. We systematically evaluate three formulations: per-test binary classification (\cls{}), execution output generation (\cwm{}), and trajectory-level patch scoring, training on identical data with controlled model sizes (4B, 8B).
3	
4	At function level, the three formulations achieve near-equivalent accuracy (\cls{} 88.43\% vs.\ \cwm{} 87.19\% at 4B, 5 seeds; Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) equivalence with trajectory-level at $p{=}0.007$). At repository level, formulation divergence amplifies to 19--26\pp{}, with \cwm{} falling below majority baseline. Cross-model validation with DeepSeek-Coder reveals a formulation $\times$ model interaction: repo-level \cwm{} degradation is formulation-inherent (both families show \cwm{} $\gg$ \cls{} performance drop from function to repo level), but its magnitude is model-contingent (Qwen3: ${\sim}$5/22\pp{} \cls{}/\cwm{} degradation; DeepSeek: ${\sim}$12/25\pp{}). \cwm{} additionally exhibits fragility at repo level along two dimensions: format non-compliance (54--74\% unparseable outputs) and higher seed variance at repo level (preliminary data: ${\sim}$5\pp{} range vs.\ \cls{}'s ${\sim}$2\pp{}).
5	
6	Two findings generalize across conditions. First, per-test classification provides diagnostic granularity (which specific tests fail) at equivalent trajectory-level accuracy at function level, with the advantage concentrating in instances with $\geq$2 failing tests (31\% of instances, 55\% of oracle advantage). Second, formulations exhibit complementary error patterns: an oracle ensemble reaches 90.63\%. This motivates complexity-aware routing rather than a single universal formulation.
7	\end{abstract}
